Analysis · National Assembly · 1988 – 2024

Islam & the Ballotدین اور دستور

Religio-political parties — those whose central platform is the political enforcement of Islam — have contested every party-based general election in Pakistan. Their combined general-seat vote has moved in a band of roughly 2–12%, peaking when the maslak (sub-sect) traditions unite on one ticket, and splitting again when they don't. Since 2018 a second engine has appeared: the Barelvi vote, mobilised by Tehreek-e-Labbaik Pakistan, now rivals the older Deobandi bloc led by JUI-F.

Vote share by sectarian tradition, 1988–2024

Share of valid votes for National Assembly general seats. Columns stack the five traditions plus cross-sect alliances (MMA 2002 & 2018; MDM 1993). Hover any segment for the parties behind it.

The series starts in 1988, the first election with clean party-level counts: in 1977 the religious parties (JUI, JUP, JI) fielded joint candidates under the nine-party PNA's single symbol, so their votes cannot be separated from the alliance's secular components (the count was also disputed); 1985 was held on a non-party basis. JI boycotted 1997 and 2008; Tehreek-e-Jafaria boycotted 1990; PAT (counted Barelvi) boycotted 2008–2018.

Provincial pattern

Combined religio-political share of the valid vote by province. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is the durable heartland — with FATA, 42.5% in 2002 — with Balochistan second and Punjab the swing market that TLP opened after 2017. Sindh's religious vote is overwhelmingly a Karachi phenomenon: split it out and the rest of Sindh rarely clears 4% before 2018. KP includes ex-FATA seats from 2018 (merger); Islamabad omitted from the chart (1–3 seats).

The 1997 and 2008 dips partly reflect boycotts (JI both years; PAT and others in 2008), not only lost support. When a sect or party is selected, a zero can mean it did not contest under that label in that election (e.g. MMA outside 2002 and 2018).

Reading the numbers

Unity is the multiplier. The two best religio-political results — 12.4% in 2002 and 9.8% in 2018 — are the two elections with a broad alliance or a new mass entrant. When the MMA (JUI-F, JI, JUP, JUI-S, Islami Tehreek) pooled candidates in 2002 it converted 11.3% of votes into 45 general seats and government in KP. The same parties running apart in 2013 took 6.8% and a handful of seats.

The Barelvi awakening is the biggest structural change since 2002. Barelvi parties (JUP tradition) polled under 3% through the 1990s and were nearly extinct by 2013 (0.3%). TLP took 4.2% in its first general election (2018) and 4.9% in 2024 — now the largest single religio-political party by votes, ahead of JUI-F — yet has never won an NA general seat: its vote is broad but shallow, second/third place across urban Punjab and Karachi.

The Deobandi bloc converts votes to seats; the Barelvi bloc doesn't. JUI-F's vote is geographically concentrated (Pashtun belt of KP and northern Balochistan), so ~4% of the national vote reliably yields seats. TLP's ~5% is spread across hundreds of Punjab seats and yields none — a textbook first-past-the-post concentration effect.

Shia and Ahl-e-Hadith electoral politics are niche. The Shia vote elects the odd seat where the community is a local majority (Kurram: MWM won NA-37 in 2024); Ahl-e-Hadith parties (incl. the Milli Muslim League lineage: AAT 2018, PMML 2024) poll ≈0.3%.

Candidate effects cut both ways. Some striking seat-level shares are electables wearing a religious ticket (Noor Alam Khan's 57% for JUI-F in Peshawar-I, 2024) rather than ideological votes — and conversely, the religious vote in many seats leaks to mainstream parties that co-opt religious planks (Nawaz-era PML-N's Punjab clerical networks, PTI's religious framing). The series here measures party label, not religiosity of the electorate.

Method & classification

A party is counted as religio-political if the political enforcement or defence of Islam is its primary platform (the convention used by PILDAT/Gallup Pakistan election reports and the academic literature, and consistent with Wikipedia's Islamic political parties in Pakistan category — minus Muslim-named but non-clerical parties such as the PML variants, PTI or AML). Classification by maslak:

TraditionParties counted (label as on ballot)
DeobandiJUI (all factions: F, S/Sami, H, Nazryati, Rabita), Islami Jamhoori Mahaz (1993, JUI-F-led), Pakistan Rah-e-Haq Party (ASWJ front, 2018–24)
BarelviJUP (Noorani, Niazi), TLP, Tehreek-e-Labbaik Islam, Sunni Tehreek, Sunni Ittehad Council, Markazi JUP, Nizam-e-Mustafa Party, PAT (Minhaj-ul-Quran; Barelvi-rooted, flagged)
JI (Islamist)Jamaat-e-Islami and its 1993 front, Pakistan Islami Front — formally cross-sect (Maududist)
ShiaTNFJ / Tehreek-e-Jafaria / Islami Tehreek, Pakistan Shia Political Party, Majlis Wahdat-e-Muslimeen
Ahl-e-HadithJamiat Ahle Hadith (Elahi Zaheer), Allah-o-Akbar Tehreek (2018), Pakistan Markazi Muslim League (2024)
Cross-sectMMA (2002: 11.3%; 2018: 4.9%) — Deobandi-led with JI, JUP and Shia components; Muttahida Deeni Mahaz (1993)

Exclusions. Mixed alliances that contained religious parties alongside secular ones are excluded because their vote cannot be decomposed: PNA (1977), IJI (1988–90, contained JI), PDA (1990, contained TNFJ), PAI (1988, contained JUP). This makes 1988–1993 a lower bound on the religious vote. The 2024 Sunni Ittehad Council figure (0.08%) is the party's own vote; PTI-backed independents joined SIC only after polling day. General (directly elected) seats only; reserved seats excluded. Unclassified minor labels (<0.3% combined, e.g. 1997 "MIP") are not counted.

Data. 1988–1997 and 2024: ECP result compilations digitised for this site; 2002–2018: Colin Cookman's consolidated ECP candidate dataset; 2018/2024 maps drawn on this site's digitised delimitations.
